lead.text: For a typical customer (a West Virginia customer with no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage, such as 180 daytime minutes) the model predicts about {{C001.risk.from|pct}} chance of leaving; it adds a set of usage and plan terms to a part for customers with low daytime use and service calls, a gate for many service calls, a voice-mail part and a few state offsets.

sentences.text: Through this sum alone, the customer's state and total international charge barely change the predicted chance that a customer leaves: for a typical customer, total international charge going from {{C054.statement.change.from}} to {{C054.statement.change.to}} (with the international minutes moved along, as in the data) leaves it at about {{C054.risk.to|pct}}.
Both also act through the parts below, where they matter more.
These usage and plan terms add up independently.

More daytime minutes raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves steadily through these terms: for a typical customer, from {{C065.risk.from|pct}} at {{C065.statement.change.from}} to about {{C065.risk.to|pct}} at {{C065.statement.change.to}} (with the daytime charge, which the model ignores, moved along as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.
An international plan raises it for a typical customer from about {{C066.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C066.risk.to|pct}}.

Higher evening charge and more evening minutes each raise it in an uneven way, from about {{C067.risk.from|pct}} at {{C067.statement.change.from}} to about {{C067.risk.to|pct}} at {{C067.statement.change.to}} of evening charge (with the evening minutes moved along, as in the data).

This part combines daytime minutes, customer-service calls, evening charge and international charge in a way that does not simply add up, and the calls-and-evening-charge piece inside it acts on {{C127.statement.n_active|d}} of {{C127.statement.n|d}} training customers.

Through this part, fewer daytime minutes raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way while daytime minutes stay below about {{C114.statement.threshold}} (between {{C114.shape.point.spread_text[0]}} and {{C114.shape.point.spread_text[1]}} for different customers; for {{C114.statement.support_check.exceptions|d}} of the {{C114.statement.support_check.n|d}} training customers it still acts above that): for a typical customer, going from {{C114.statement.change.from}} to {{C114.statement.change.to}} (with the daytime charge moved along, as in the data) moves it from about {{C114.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C114.risk.to|pct}}.

In the whole model, more daytime minutes raise the predicted chance, and even more so if total evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars, in a curve that is lowest at about {{C112.shape.groups[0].points_text.turning}} and higher either side: for a typical customer with that evening charge (and the evening minutes such customers have in the data), going from {{C112.statement.change.from}} to {{C112.statement.change.to}} raises it from about {{C112.statement.stronger_group.risk_from|pct}} to about {{C112.statement.stronger_group.risk_to|pct}}, against about {{C112.statement.weaker_group.risk_from|pct}} to about {{C112.statement.weaker_group.risk_to|pct}} at or below that charge.

More customer-service calls raise it, slowly at first and then faster, and even more so if the customer is in South Dakota: for a typical customer, going from 0 to 3 calls moves it from about {{C122.statement.stronger_group.risk_from|pct}} to about {{C122.statement.stronger_group.risk_to|pct}} in South Dakota and from about {{C122.statement.weaker_group.risk_from|pct}} to about {{C122.statement.weaker_group.risk_to|pct}} elsewhere.

Through this part, a voice-mail plan lowers the predicted chance that a customer leaves, from about {{C129.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C129.risk.to|pct}} for a typical customer (with the voice-mail messages moved to the 29 such customers have in the data).
In the whole model, a voice-mail plan takes the typical customer from about {{C018.risk.from|pct}} to {{C018.risk.to|pct}} (again with the messages moved along).

This gate adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves only from 4 calls to customer service upwards (checked for all {{C135.statement.support_check.n|d}} training customers, with {{C135.statement.support_check.exceptions|d}} exceptions), and it acts on {{C136.statement.n_active|d}} of {{C136.statement.n|d}} training customers.

For a typical customer it acts on (an Idaho customer with 4 calls), it raises the predicted chance from about {{C136.risk.from|pct}} without the gate to about {{C136.risk.to|pct}} with it; {{C136.statement.outcome_in_group.positives|d}} of these {{C136.statement.outcome_in_group.n|d}} customers left.
Through this gate, a typical customer it acts on gets about {{C134.risk.to|pct}} outside West Virginia and about {{C134.risk.from|pct}} in West Virginia.

These state offsets move the predicted chance by small amounts for a few states: for a typical customer, Tennessee raises it from about {{C141.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C141.risk.to|pct}} and Nevada lowers it from about {{C142.risk.from|pct}} to about {{C142.risk.to|pct}}.
